Can You Still See Nature?

When was the last time you truly listened to the wind moving through the leaves, or noticed the intricate veins of a fallen leaf? For most of us living in dense urban jungles, the answer is far too long ago. We have traded the smell of damp soil for filtered air, and the chorus of insects for the hum of air conditioning. In doing so, we have lost our ecological literacy. We desperately want to "save the environment," but we have forgotten how to even see it. True environmental action does not begin in a policy room; it begins at eye level with a seedling. To solve the overarching environmental crisis, we must stop treating nature as an abstract problem and start experiencing it as a home to be cherished.

The consequences of this disconnect are profound. Overarching environmental issues—from biodiversity collapse to extreme weather—are essentially the symptoms of a system we no longer understand. Because of this lack of true understanding, these issues are easily re-enchanted in our minds, unintentionally or deliberately, by those with vested interests. Some groups deliberately shift the focus to protect their own agendas, blocking us from the truth. Let me show you something surprising: we passionately defend the rainforest, yet ignore that marine phytoplankton—organisms we cannot even see—generate over half of the oxygen we breathe. We quantify our progress in GDP, completely ignoring the silent massacre of biodiversity happening at a rate 1,000 times faster than natural extinction. This is the reality of our blind spots. We cannot simply react with panic or apply generic fixes; only when we truly comprehend exactly what is unfolding within our natural environment can we identify the genuinely appropriate and effective solutions. We cannot solve a crisis we barely comprehend.

I am not telling these stories to shout hollow slogans, but as reminders of what we have long ignored. Imagine a Sunday morning in Hong Kong. An elderly resident, Mr. Chan, used to watch sparrows nest in the cracks of his aging tenement building. When a glass high-rise replaced it, the birds vanished. He felt a quiet grief, even without knowing the term "biodiversity loss." Then, a group of students visited. They didn't lecture him with abstract data; they sat with him, opened a citizen science app, and helped him record the few remaining sparrows in a nearby park. Suddenly, his local knowledge had value. He became the neighborhood's unofficial bird guardian. This is the power of placebased education: it turns a distant, overwhelming issue into a personal, tangible one.

Fostering this eco-friendly awareness is not a task reserved for policymakers; it is a call to action for all of us. First, we can demand that schools break down the walls of the classroom. Instead of merely analyzing data on screens, we can petition to integrate "ecological literacy" into the curriculum, turning local parks into living laboratories. Second, we can actively participate in citizen science. By using mobile apps to document local flora and fauna—like the declining urban sparrows (Ming Pao, 2024)—ordinary citizens can contribute verifiable data to biodiversity databases. The overarching environmental crisis will not be solved in a sterile laboratory or a distant colony. It will be solved in the quiet moments when a city dweller touches damp soil or pauses to listen to the wind. This is a deeply hopeful endeavor. Every time we step outside to identify a native plant or record a local bird, we are not just collecting data; we are actively restoring our bond with the living world. Such profound understanding and intimate connection will naturally translate into a powerful, collective force—one that can drive real systemic change and healing our planet. We do not need to escape this planet to find paradise; we need to notice the one still blooming outside our

windows. Let us step away from our screens and walk out into the wild corners of our neighborhoods.
